summary: A feature profile of Jenna O'Connor, a local environmental activist in Farmland County, who campaigns against soil contamination from heavy metals, pesticides, and industrial waste. The note covers its effects on microbial diversity, pollinators, and farm yields, along with her education and lobbying work, a successful County Council resolution, phytoremediation at Bill McKenna's farm, and technology and partnerships aiding recovery.
one_line: Profile of activist Jenna O'Connor's campaign against soil contamination in Farmland County and its harm to agriculture and biodiversity, plus remediation efforts.
key_facts: Jenna O'Connor is a local environmental activist in Farmland County; the interview takes place on September 5, 2023.
Soil contamination occurs when hazardous substances such as heavy metals, pesticides, and industrial waste seep into the soil.
O'Connor's activism began when farmer Bill McKenna saw his crop yields decline; testing found high heavy metal levels traced to a now-defunct battery recycling plant.

A study published October 15, 2023 by Dr. Alice Forrester of the Farmland Agricultural Institute found persistent organic pollutants (POPs) reduce soil microbial diversity, hurting nutrient cycling, fertility, and crop health.
A September 28, 2023 report by the Environmental Monitoring Center recorded a 30% drop in the local bee population over the last two years.
Pollinators are crucial for about three-quarters of crop species.
O'Connor regularly conducts soil health workshops at a local school and works with schools and local governments on citizen monitoring programs.
On November 20, 2023, the County Council passed a resolution to increase funding for soil testing and remediation, which O'Connor sees as only a first step.
McKenna is restoring his farm's fertility using phytoremediation, a process in which plants extract toxins from the soil.

Partnerships among farmers, environmental groups, and agricultural experts introduced organic farming and soil conservation; improved soil quality and a small return of native species were reported on February 12, 2024.
Tech startup CleanEarth Solutions launched an app combining satellite imagery and ground data to detect soil contamination hotspots.
O'Connor was invited to speak at the National Soil Summit in April 2024.
